title: Physical and Chemical Changes
seo_title: Grade 6 Science: Physical and Chemical Changes Worksheets (MATATAG)
standard_text: Physical changes change the size, shape or state of a material but make no new substance; chemical changes make new substances, shown by color change, gas, heat or light; some changes can be reversed and others cannot. (summary of the MATATAG Science curriculum, Grade 6, Quarter 1: Materials)
meta_desc: Free Grade 6 Science worksheets (MATATAG, Quarter 1: Materials): physical or chemical?, signs of chemical change, reversible and irreversible, changes in daily life and change investigations. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: A chemical change makes a new substance.
key_sub: Physical changes (melting, cutting, dissolving) can often be reversed; chemical changes usually cannot.
body_html:
How to think about it

In a physical change, the substance stays the same. In a chemical change, a new substance forms.

  • Physical changes: melting, freezing, cutting, crushing, dissolving.
  • Chemical changes: burning, rusting, cooking, rotting.
  • Signs of a chemical change: gas bubbles, a new color or smell, light or heat given off, a solid forming.
Example

Is burning toast physical or chemical?

new black substance

cannot change back

Answer: chemical

Example

Is dissolving salt in water physical or chemical?

evaporate the water to get the salt back

Answer: physical

Common mistakes

  • Thinking every change of color is a chemical change.
  • Thinking dissolving makes the substance disappear.
  • Thinking chemical changes are always dangerous.

faq.q: How can you tell a chemical change happened?
faq.a: Look for a new substance: bubbles of gas, a new color or smell, light or heat, or a solid forming in a liquid.
No. Melting changes the state, but the substance is still the same.

faq.q: Why do chemical changes matter for the environment?
faq.a: Burning fuels and some factory processes make pollution, so waste must be treated and reduced.

items.e: A copper roof turning green makes a new substance. The others only change shape, size or state, or mix things.

items.q: Which is a chemical change?

items.q: What kind of change is fireworks exploding?

items.q: Which is a physical change?
items.e: Mixing sand and pebbles does not make a new substance. The others all make new substances.

items.q: Why is recycling aluminum cans useful?
c: Melting and reshaping cans uses less energy than mining new aluminum.

items.q: Which is a chemical change?

items.e: Food being digested in your stomach makes a new substance. The others only change shape, size or state, or mix things.

items.q: What kind of change is chopping wood for a fire?

items.e: Chopping wood for a fire changes the shape, size, state or mixture, but the substances stay the same.

items.q: Which is a chemical change?
items.e: A candle wick burning makes a new substance. The others only change shape, size or state, or mix things.

items.q: Why is cooking an egg a chemical change?
c: New substances form and it cannot change back.
It is still a raw egg.
items.e: Heat changes the proteins in the egg.

items.q: Which is a chemical change?

items.q: Which is a chemical change?
items.e: Milk going sour makes a new substance. The others only change shape, size or state, or mix things.

items.q: Which is a physical change?

items.q: What kind of change is a silver spoon tarnishing?
c: a physical change, because only the state changes
a physical change, because only the shape changes
a chemical change, because a new substance forms
items.e: A silver spoon tarnishing makes a new substance with new properties, so it is a chemical change.

items.q: Which change can be easily reversed?
items.e: Ice can melt back into water.

items.q: Mixing baking soda and vinegar makes bubbles. What kind of change is this?
items.e: Carbon dioxide gas forms.

items.q: What kind of change is water boiling in a pot?
c: a physical change, because no new substance forms
a chemical change, because a new substance forms
a chemical change, because it gives off light
items.e: Water boiling in a pot changes the shape, size, state or mixture, but the substances stay the same.

items.q: Which is a physical change?
items.e: Melting butter in a pan does not make a new substance. The others all make new substances.

items.q: Which is a physical change?
items.e: Crushing an aluminum can does not make a new substance. The others all make new substances.

items.q: Which is a chemical change?
items.e: Frying an egg makes a new substance. The others only change shape, size or state, or mix things.

items.q: Which is a chemical change?
items.e: Bread dough rising with yeast makes a new substance. The others only change shape, size or state, or mix things.

items.q: Two clear liquids are mixed and a cloudy white solid appears. What evidence of a chemical change is there?
items.e: The observation shows a new solid, which is evidence that a new substance formed.

items.q: Which is a sign that a new material has been made: heat or light is given out, the material gets colder, the material is cut into pieces or the solid melts into a liquid?
c: the solid melts into a liquid
the material is cut into pieces
heat or light is given out
items.e: Gas, color change, heat and light are signs of an irreversible change.

items.q: An antacid tablet is dropped in water and fizzes. What evidence of a chemical change is there?
items.e: The observation shows gas bubbles, which is evidence that a new substance formed.

items.q: A cake batter rises and turns brown in the oven. What evidence of a chemical change is there?
items.e: The observation shows gas and a new color, which is evidence that a new substance formed.

items.q: Which is a sign that a new material has been made: a new smell is made, the material changes shape, the material dissolves and disappears from view or the material gets colder?
c: the material dissolves and disappears from view
items.e: Gas, color change, heat and light are signs of an irreversible change.

items.q: Which observation is evidence that a new substance may have formed?
c: Bubbles of gas form when two substances are mixed.
items.e: Gas from mixing, a new color, a temperature change, light, a new solid or a new smell are signs of a chemical change. Shape and state changes are physical.

items.q: A nail left outside turns red-brown and flaky. What evidence of a chemical change is there?
c: a new color and a new solid
items.e: The observation shows a new color and a new solid, which is evidence that a new substance formed.

items.q: A match is struck and it flames. What evidence of a chemical change is there?
items.e: The observation shows light and heat, which is evidence that a new substance formed.

items.q: A hand warmer pack is opened and gets hot. What evidence of a chemical change is there?
items.e: The observation shows a temperature change, which is evidence that a new substance formed.

items.q: Is plaster of Paris setting a reversible or an irreversible change?
c: it is only a change of state
it is the same as dissolving
items.e: A new material is made, so it cannot easily be changed back.

items.q: The roof of an old farm shed goes rusty. Is this a reversible or an irreversible change?
c: a change that only happens in a laboratory
items.e: It cannot be undone, and new materials are made.

items.q: Wax drips from a candle and hardens. Is this a reversible or an irreversible change?
c: a change that only happens in a laboratory
items.e: It can be undone, so no new material is made.

items.q: Is boiling water into steam a reversible or an irreversible change?
items.e: Changes of state, dissolving and mixing can be reversed.

items.q: How can a factory reduce the harm from chemical changes?
c: by treating waste so it does not pollute water and air
items.e: Waste can be treated or reused.

items.q: Is dissolving salt in water a reversible or an irreversible change?
items.e: Changes of state, dissolving and mixing can be reversed.

items.q: Which change can be reversed: concrete setting hard, frying an egg, melting butter or striking a match?
items.e: Burning, cooking, rusting and fizzing reactions make new materials.

items.q: Which change makes a new material: condensation forming on a cold window, dissolving salt in water, milk going sour or mixing sand and water?
c: condensation forming on a cold window
items.e: Burning, cooking, rusting and fizzing reactions make new materials.

items.q: Which is a sign that a chemical change may have happened?
c: a new smell, gas bubbles or a color change
items.e: New substances can give off gas, light or heat.

items.q: Is dissolving sugar in water a reversible or an irreversible change?
items.e: Changes of state, dissolving and mixing can be reversed.

items.q: Damper dough is cooked in hot coals. Is this a reversible or an irreversible change?

items.e: It cannot be undone, and new materials are made.

items.q: Which change makes a new material: an iron gate rusting, melting candle wax, melting chocolate or mixing sand and water?
items.e: Burning, cooking, rusting and fizzing reactions make new materials.

it is the same as dissolving

items.q: Anzac cookie mixture is baked in the oven. Is this a reversible or an irreversible change?
c: a change that only happens in a laboratory
items.e: It cannot be undone, and new materials are made.

items.q: Is melting candle wax a reversible or an irreversible change?
items.e: Changes of state, dissolving and mixing can be reversed.

items.q: Butter melts on hot toast. Is this a reversible or an irreversible change?
c: a change that only happens in a laboratory
items.e: It can be undone, so no new material is made.

items.q: Which change can be reversed: baking a cake, melting chocolate, mixing vinegar and bicarbonate of soda or toasting bread?
c: mixing vinegar and bicarbonate of soda
items.e: Burning, cooking, rusting and fizzing reactions make new materials.

items.q: Fruit peel rots in a compost bin. Is this a reversible or an irreversible change?
c: a change that only happens in a laboratory
items.e: It cannot be undone, and new materials are made.

items.q: Wattle seeds are roasted on a campfire and turn dark brown. Is this a reversible or an irreversible change?
c: a change that only happens in a laboratory
items.e: It cannot be undone, and new materials are made.

items.q: Which change can be reversed: an iron gate rusting, baking a cake, burning a candle wick or melting butter?
items.e: Burning, cooking, rusting and fizzing reactions make new materials.

items.q: Which is a physical change to a piece of paper?
c: letting it turn yellow in the sun for years
items.e: Folding changes the shape only. It is still paper.

items.q: Which is a physical change?
items.e: No new substance forms.

items.q: Which is not a sign of a physical change?
c: a change from liquid to gas when heated
a gas forming when two liquids mix
items.e: A new gas from mixing can mean a new substance. Changing shape, size or state are physical changes.

items.q: Why is burning dangerous to investigate?
c: It gives out heat and flames that can cause burns and fires.
items.e: Only with adult supervision.

items.q: Can a cooked egg be uncooked?
c: No, cooking is an irreversible change.
items.e: The proteins have changed for good.

items.q: Why is melting ice a physical change?
c: It is still water, just in a different state.
items.e: Changes of state are physical.

items.q: When wood burns, what new materials are made?
c: ash, smoke and gases such as carbon dioxide
items.e: Burning needs oxygen.

items.q: Lemonade powder is stirred into water and the water turns yellow. Is a new substance formed?
c: No. The powder dissolves and colors the water, making a mixture.
items.e: The powder only dissolves. The color comes from the powder spreading through the water.

items.q: What happens when vinegar is added to bicarbonate of soda?
c: It fizzes and makes carbon dioxide gas.
It turns into salt water only.
items.e: A new gas is made.

items.q: Sugar dissolves in water. Why is this a physical change?
c: The sugar is still sugar; the water can evaporate to get it back.
items.e: Dissolving makes a mixture. Evaporate the water and the sugar crystals are left behind.

items.q: What is rust?
c: a new material formed when iron reacts with water and oxygen
items.e: Iron oxide.

items.q: Salt water is heated until the water is gone and salt is left. What does this show about dissolving salt?
c: It was a physical change: the salt was still there.
items.e: The same salt comes back, so no new substance had formed.

items.q: Rust forms on a bike left outside. What causes this change?
c: iron reacting with oxygen and water
items.e: Rust is a new substance.

items.q: Water boils and bubbles form. Is this evidence of a new substance?
c: No. The bubbles are water vapor, the same substance as a gas.
Yes, the bubbles are a new gas.
items.e: Boiling is a change of state. The bubbles are water in its gas form.

items.q: Angelo dissolves sugar in warm and cold water. Which is a fair way to compare them?
c: use the same amount of sugar, water and stirring
use more sugar in the cold water
use different cups of different sizes
items.e: Change only the temperature.

items.q: Why should an adult light a candle or heat food in a class investigation?
c: to keep everyone safe from burns and fire
items.e: Safety comes first.

items.q: A learner says dissolving salt is irreversible because the salt disappears. How could you show it is reversible?
c: Evaporate the water and get the salt back.
items.e: Evidence.

items.q: A sealed bag holds 80 g of vinegar and a small cup with 20 g of baking soda. The bag is tipped so they mix and the bag puffs up. What is the total mass now?
items.e: A new gas forms, but the bag is sealed, so nothing gets out: 80 + 20 = 100 g. The particles are rearranged, not destroyed.

items.q: Nico wants to find out which liquid makes iron nails rust fastest. What should he keep the same?
c: only the color of the tubes
the kind of nail, the amount of liquid and the time
items.e: Only the liquid should change.

items.q: Two cups of milk are left out, one in a warm room and one in the refrigerator. Which will most likely smell sour first?
c: the milk in the warm room
items.e: Souring is a chemical change made by tiny living things. It happens faster when it is warm.

items.q: Which safety rule is most important when testing mixtures in class?
c: Wear safety goggles and never taste the mixtures.
Mix as many things as possible.
items.e: Unknown mixtures can be harmful. Goggles protect your eyes, and you should never taste them.

items.q: Emmanuel puts a steel wool pad in a jar with a little water and seals it. After a week it is orange. Why does he also keep a dry steel wool pad in a sealed jar?
c: to see if water is needed for rusting
items.e: Comparing wet and dry steel wool shows whether water affects rusting.

items.q: A sealed bag holds 50 g of vinegar and a small cup with 15 g of baking soda. The bag is tipped so they mix and the bag puffs up. What is the total mass now?
items.e: A new gas forms, but the bag is sealed, so nothing gets out: 50 + 15 = 65 g. The particles are rearranged, not destroyed.

items.q: A sealed bag holds 100 g of vinegar and a small cup with 10 g of baking soda. The bag is tipped so they mix and the bag puffs up. What is the total mass now?
items.e: A new gas forms, but the bag is sealed, so nothing gets out: 100 + 10 = 110 g. The particles are rearranged, not destroyed.

items.q: Hazel heats 20 g of chocolate until it melts, then cools it. It weighs 20 g again. What does this show?
c: Chocolate gains mass when it melts.
Melting is reversible and no material is lost.
items.e: The same material changed state.

items.q: Which question can be answered by mixing two substances and observing?
c: Does mixing vinegar and baking soda make a new substance?
items.e: You can test it in class: mix them, observe the bubbles and compare properties.

items.q: A sealed bag holds 150 g of vinegar and a small cup with 10 g of baking soda. The bag is tipped so they mix and the bag puffs up. What is the total mass now?
items.e: A new gas forms, but the bag is sealed, so nothing gets out: 150 + 10 = 160 g. The particles are rearranged, not destroyed.

items.q: Why do scientists repeat an investigation several times?
c: to check that the results are reliable
items.e: If the same results happen again and again, you can trust them more.

items.q: In the balloon investigation, why use the same amount of vinegar each time?
c: so only the amount of bicarbonate changes
items.e: Fair test.

items.q: Rose mixes 3 spoonfuls of baking soda with vinegar and gets a lot of bubbles. With 1 spoonful she gets fewer bubbles. What did she change?
items.e: Only the amount of baking soda changed, so that is the variable she tested.

items.q: Which observation would show that rusting is faster in salt water than in fresh water?
c: Nails in fresh water stay longer.
Both nails are the same size.
Nails in salt water get more rust in the same number of days.
items.e: Compare the amount of rust after the same time. More rust means a faster chemical change.

items.q: A sealed bag holds 150 g of vinegar and a small cup with 15 g of baking soda. The bag is tipped so they mix and the bag puffs up. What is the total mass now?

items.q: Lance wants to know if salt makes ice melt faster. Which is the best plan?
c: Use a big cube with salt and a small cube without.
Put the same size ice cubes on two plates, add salt to one, and time both.
items.e: Change only one thing (the salt) and compare with a cube that has no salt.
